Possible evidence: S1 human-review routing. Confirm the actual customer need and why you chose that safeguard; do not infer auditor requirements from the presence of a review step.

rapid_fire.q: Region vs AZ vs edge location?
rapid_fire.a: A Region is a geographic area with multiple isolated AZs. An AZ is one or more data centers with independent power and networking. An edge location is a CloudFront and Route 53 point of presence near users for caching and DNS.

rapid_fire.q: How do you make a web app highly available on AWS?
rapid_fire.a: Clarify the availability target and failure scope. Use stateless capacity across at least 2 AZs behind an ALB, a suitable Multi-AZ database, health checks, and enough surviving capacity. Make requests idempotent and test reconnects after failover. Backups plus restore drills protect against accidental deletion/corruption; replication is not a backup. Regional DR depends on business RPO/RTO, not an automatic requirement.

rapid_fire.q: Security group vs NACL?
rapid_fire.a: Security groups are stateful, attach to instances or network interfaces, and only allow. NACLs are stateless, attach to subnets, have ordered allow and deny rules, so return traffic must be allowed explicitly.

rapid_fire.q: Public vs private subnet? What does a NAT Gateway do?
rapid_fire.a: A public subnet has an Internet Gateway route; direct IPv4 access also requires a public IP and allowed traffic. A public NAT gateway lets private workloads initiate internet traffic; responses return through the NAT, while unsolicited inbound traffic is blocked. Check both directions through routes, security groups and stateless NACLs. S3/DynamoDB gateway endpoints can avoid NAT for those services; endpoint policies do not grant all required permissions.

rapid_fire.q: ALB vs NLB? When API Gateway?
rapid_fire.a: Use ALB for HTTP host/path routing and NLB for transport-layer TCP/UDP/TLS, static IPs, or supported PrivateLink services. Use API Gateway for an API-management requirement; REST and HTTP APIs have different features and prices. REST usage plans/API keys meter clients; API keys are not user authentication. Ask who authenticates requests, where TLS terminates, and whether the origin is reachable around the front door.

rapid_fire.q: S3 storage classes and lifecycle. How do you make S3 cheaper?
rapid_fire.a: Standard for hot data, Intelligent-Tiering when access is unknown, Standard-IA and One Zone-IA for infrequent access, Glacier tiers for archive. Lifecycle rules move or expire objects; also expire old versions and incomplete multipart uploads.

rapid_fire.q: EBS vs EFS vs S3?
rapid_fire.a: EBS is block storage scoped to one AZ, usually attached to one instance; supported Multi-Attach io1/io2 volumes require coordinated writes. EFS is shared NFS with Regional or One Zone resilience. S3 is object storage through APIs. Pick from the application access protocol, sharing and recovery requirements; a mounted volume or multi-AZ copy is not a tested backup.

rapid_fire.q: RDS Multi-AZ vs read replica?
rapid_fire.a: Specify the deployment: Multi-AZ DB instance has one synchronous non-readable standby for failover. Multi-AZ DB cluster has a writer and two readable standbys in three AZs for supported MySQL/PostgreSQL versions. Separate read replicas generally replicate asynchronously for read scaling; promotion and replication support depend on engine.

rapid_fire.q: DynamoDB vs RDS? What is a hot partition?
rapid_fire.a: RDS/Aurora fits joins, flexible relational queries, and relational transactions. DynamoDB also supports transactions within an account/Region; choose it for designed key-value/document access patterns. Tables and LSIs can provide strong reads; GSIs are eventually consistent. A popular key can overload one partition even when total capacity looks sufficient. Example: use a designed user-ID lookup for sessions; benchmark SQL for changing finance-report joins. Write sharding adds read/aggregation work.

rapid_fire.q: Lambda limits and cold starts. When not to use Lambda?
rapid_fire.a: 15-minute max runtime, up to 10 GB memory, payload limits. Cold starts add latency for new environments; reduce with provisioned concurrency or SnapStart where the runtime and configuration support it. Avoid it for long jobs, steady very high throughput, or GPU work.

rapid_fire.q: ECS vs EKS vs Fargate?
rapid_fire.a: ECS is AWS's simpler orchestrator; EKS is managed Kubernetes for teams already on it or needing portability. Fargate is serverless compute for either, with no nodes to manage.

rapid_fire.q: SQS vs SNS vs EventBridge vs Kinesis?
rapid_fire.a: SQS buffers work; competing consumers share work rather than each receiving a copy. SNS fans out; separate SQS queues let each subscriber process independently. EventBridge routes events; Kinesis provides retained streams and replay with ordering scoped to a shard. SQS FIFO orders by message group and deduplicates sends within 5 minutes; external side effects still need durable idempotency. Use bounded backoff with jitter, visibility extension, a monitored DLQ and controlled redrive.

rapid_fire.q: IAM role vs user? What is least privilege?
rapid_fire.a: A role supplies temporary credentials; its trust policy controls who may assume it, while permissions control subsequent actions. Identify principal, action, resource and conditions. An applicable explicit deny wins. Example: a role allows s3:GetObject, but a bucket policy denies that principal outside an approved endpoint: the read is denied. Check resource/key policies, boundaries, sessions and organization policies as applicable; cross-account paths need appropriate grants on both sides.

rapid_fire.q: What is the shared responsibility model?
rapid_fire.a: AWS secures the cloud: facilities, hardware, network, hypervisor. The customer secures what is in it: data, IAM, encryption, network rules, OS patches on EC2. The line moves up as services get more managed.

rapid_fire.q: Encryption at rest vs in transit? What does KMS do?
rapid_fire.a: TLS protects data in transit; verify certificate hostname, trust and expiry at each termination point. At rest, services may use service-managed keys or KMS keys. KMS controls key operations, not application authorization. A role can have data-read access but lack required decrypt access. CloudTrail records KMS API calls; verify event selectors and data-event coverage rather than promising an audit entry for every local use of a data key.

rapid_fire.q: RPO vs RTO, and the four DR strategies?
rapid_fire.a: RPO is how much data loss you accept; RTO is how long you can be down. Cheapest to fastest: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site active/active.

rapid_fire.q: Name the 6 Well-Architected pillars.
rapid_fire.a: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, Sustainability.

rapid_fire.q: Name the 7 Rs of migration.
rapid_fire.a: Retire, Retain, Rehost, Relocate, Repurchase, Replatform, Refactor. Replacing an ERP with SaaS is Repurchase; describe your ERP project using only verified details.

rapid_fire.q: CloudWatch vs CloudTrail vs Config?
rapid_fire.a: CloudWatch supports metrics, logs, alarms and request telemetry; CloudTrail records supported AWS API/account activity; Config records supported resource configuration and evaluates rules. For a latency incident, correlate request IDs, tail latency, dependency errors and recent changes. For who deleted an S3 object, enable the required CloudTrail data events; management-event history alone will not answer every object-level question.

rapid_fire.q: How would you reduce a customer's AWS bill?
rapid_fire.a: Start with the business metric, Cost Explorer drivers, recent changes and tags. Reduce idle/oversized capacity, excess logs, storage versions and avoidable transfer/NAT before committing spend. Model baseline commitments, interruptible Spot and storage lifecycle against actual demand. Example: compare NAT charges with S3 gateway endpoints while retaining the required access controls. Validate latency and cost per successful transaction; Budgets alerts are not a guaranteed spending cap.

rapid_fire.q: What happens when you type a URL into a browser?
rapid_fire.a: Check browser/OS caches; a recursive DNS resolver uses cached answers or queries authoritative servers. For a new HTTPS connection, establish transport (usually TCP; HTTP/3 uses QUIC), then TLS validates the certificate hostname/trust and negotiates encryption. HTTP goes to the CDN or origin; cache policy determines an edge hit or a request through the ALB, application, cache and database. Existing connections can be reused. Trace DNS, connect, TLS and application time separately; Route 53 answers DNS rather than proxying the HTTP request.

rapid_fire.q: TCP vs UDP, and common HTTP status codes?
rapid_fire.a: TCP provides an ordered reliable byte stream with congestion control; UDP provides datagrams without built-in delivery or ordering guarantees. Applications can add reliability over UDP: QUIC powers HTTP/3. DNS can use UDP or TCP. For HTTP: 401 needs valid authentication; 403 is refusal; 429 is throttling; 502 can indicate an invalid upstream response; 504 is an upstream timeout. A status code narrows the investigation but does not prove the root cause.

rapid_fire.q: What is Bedrock? How would you build RAG on AWS?
rapid_fire.a: Bedrock is a managed API to foundation models with Knowledge Bases, Agents, Guardrails, and evaluation. RAG: documents in S3, a Knowledge Base chunks and embeds them into a vector store such as OpenSearch Serverless, retrieves chunks with server-side authorization derived from trusted identity, and the model answers with citations. Guardrails do not enforce document permissions; scope caches to authorization and verify inference routing and retention.

rapid_fire.q: How do you choose between a large and a small model for a customer?
rapid_fire.a: Start from the task and an evaluation set, not the model. Try the smallest model that passes, compare cost per request and latency, and move up only when quality fails. ModelScope is your evidence: INT4 kept MMLU within a point at 62% less memory.

roleplay_rules: Ask before proposing: business goal, current setup, constraints, timeline, budget, compliance.
Restate the problem in their words.
Propose 1 or 2 options, each with a tradeoff and a cost direction.
Match the audience: a CFO hears cost and risk; engineers hear services and design.
Never overpromise. If unsure: "I will verify the documented behavior and agree a realistic follow-up time with you."
Close with next steps: a proof of concept, a Well-Architected review, or a follow-up meeting.

roleplays.title: Retail CTO: site goes down on peak days
roleplays.opening: I'm the CTO of a retailer. Our site goes down on peak days. What should we do?
discovery: What happens when it goes down: slow pages, errors, checkout failures?
Where does it run today, and what is the peak compared with a normal day?
Which peaks are known in advance?
What does an hour of downtime cost you?
Any constraints: budget, team size, timeline to the next peak?

options.name: Prove and relieve the bottleneck
options.tradeoff: Use request traces and a representative load test to decide whether scheduled scaling, safe caching or read capacity addresses the current failure. Faster intervention with measured limits; it may leave deeper write-path issues.

options.name: Change the constrained path
options.tradeoff: If the evidence supports it, move state out of app instances and add an atomic order/outbox handoff with idempotent workers. Evaluate a database change separately; Aurora does not automatically fix every bottleneck.

roleplays.close: Agree a pilot and load-test success criteria before the next customer peak: checkout success, tail latency, recovery behavior and unit cost.

roleplays.title: CFO: explain containers and why they matter
roleplays.opening: My engineers keep asking for budget for containers. Explain it to me and tell me why I should care.
discovery: What problem are you hoping to solve: cost, speed of releases, reliability?
How do you track infrastructure spend today?

options.name: Plain explanation
options.tradeoff: A container packages software and its dependencies consistently, helping teams deploy and share host capacity. Savings and release benefits depend on utilization, migration effort and platform operations; prove them with a pilot.

options.name: Start small
options.tradeoff: Move one service first and compare total cost per transaction, release frequency and failure recovery before committing a wider budget.

roleplays.close: Offer a one-page cost comparison after a small pilot, with numbers they can check.

roleplays.title: Bank: wants a GenAI assistant but fears data leaks
roleplays.audience: Head of digital, with security in the room
roleplays.opening: We want a GenAI assistant for our support agents, but our CISO is worried customer data will leak into a model.
discovery: Which data would the assistant need to see?
Which regulations apply, and where must data stay?
Who approves new AI use cases internally?
How would you judge the assistant is good enough?

options.name: Bedrock with RAG
options.tradeoff: Verify model terms and retention settings, invocation logging, and cross-Region inference routing against residency needs. Use approved documents with server-side entitlement filters; Guardrails are content filters, not authorization. Lower initial scope, with measurable privacy and answer-quality tests.

options.name: Agent with tools
options.tradeoff: Can look up account data through scoped Lambda tools. More useful, more to secure and evaluate.

roleplays.close: Propose a proof of concept on non-sensitive documents with an evaluation set the CISO helps define. This mirrors the human review in your S1 story.

roleplays.title: Manufacturer: data center lease ends in 9 months
roleplays.opening: Our data center lease ends in 9 months. We have 200 servers including our ERP. Can we be on AWS in time?
discovery: Which systems are critical, and which might be retired?
How much downtime can the ERP take at cutover?
What skills does your team have on AWS today?

options.name: Rehost first, modernize later
options.tradeoff: Fastest path to the deadline with Application Migration Service; keeps today's inefficiencies for now.

options.name: Mixed 7 Rs per workload
options.tradeoff: Retire and repurchase where possible, rehost the rest. More planning up front, lower long-term cost.

roleplays.close: Offer a discovery assessment and a wave plan, with the ERP in a later wave once the landing zone is proven.

roleplays.title: Startup founder: our AWS bill doubled
roleplays.opening: Our AWS bill doubled last month and I don't know why. Help.
discovery: Which services grew, per Cost Explorer?
Did anything launch or change last month?
Are resources tagged by team or environment?

options.name: Stop the bleeding
options.tradeoff: Find the top drivers, delete idle resources, set Budgets alerts. Fast, but does not prevent the next surprise.

options.name: Build cost habits
options.tradeoff: Tagging, right-sizing with Compute Optimizer, Savings Plans for baseline. Takes a few weeks, lasting savings.

roleplays.close: Agree to review Cost Explorer together this week and set a budget alert today.

roleplays.title: Healthcare startup: is AWS safe for patient data?
roleplays.audience: CTO of a small health startup
roleplays.opening: We handle patient records. Can we even use AWS, and what do we have to do?
discovery: What data do you store, and who accesses it?
Have you signed a Business Associate Addendum (BAA)?
What does your security team look like today?

options.name: Shared responsibility explained
options.tradeoff: Confirm the applicable agreement and current HIPAA-eligible services with the security/compliance owner. AWS eligibility does not make the application compliant; the customer owns access, configuration and operating controls.

options.name: Reviewable starting point
options.tradeoff: Evaluate account separation, logging, least privilege, key management, monitored threat detection and incident response against the actual data flow. Each control needs an owner and evidence.

roleplays.close: Offer a security-focused architecture review and point them to HIPAA-eligible services only.

roleplays.title: Partner with sales on a financial migration recommendation
roleplays.audience: Sales colleague, customer engineer, and finance executive
roleplays.opening: The customer wants a migration commitment before we have tested their data and downtime constraints. Sales needs a credible next step. How would you help?
discovery: Which customer outcome defines success: reconciliation effort, processing time, accuracy, or availability?
What are the cutover window, data dependencies, approval process, and rollback criteria?
What evidence do the customer engineer and finance executive each need before committing?

options.name: Evidence-based pilot
options.tradeoff: Agree a representative synthetic or approved-data pilot with the customer and sales colleague. Define success criteria, validation owners, cost drivers, and a review date. A pilot adds discovery time but tests the riskiest assumptions.

options.name: Full migration commitment now
options.tradeoff: A faster commercial commitment carries untested correctness and downtime risk. Explain what is unknown and propose conditions for a responsible commitment; do not imply guarantees from a diagram.

roleplays.close: To the engineer: explain validation, retry handling, reconciliation, cutover, and rollback. To the executive: explain the customer outcome, remaining risk, and pilot decision. Align with sales on a documented next step; measure the value delivered to the customer.
